title: Building an Explorable 3D World by Planning It First
hook: Text-to-3D usually yields one pretty scene. WorldClaw has planning agents write a spec — regions, terrain, assets, materials — then builds coarse-to-fine, so the world stays editable.
key_points: The hard part of open-world generation is doing three things at once: global spatial coherence, rich local detail, and explicit assets you can edit and reuse afterwards.
Planning agents first translate the text prompt into a structured specification of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations.
A globally coherent terrain foundation is built from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative or procedural materials, and a region-aware height field.
Detail-demanding regions get terrain-conditioned compositions, reconstructed as editable textured meshes with their placement on the terrain recovered.
Render-based agents then refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts.
The output is instance-level editable assets inside a consistent global terrain — not a single baked scene.
content_html: Ask a generative system for "a windswept coastal region with a ruined fort", and you can usually get a good-looking scene. Getting a world — large, freely explorable, coherent at the horizon and detailed underfoot, with assets you can still open and edit — is a different problem, because those requirements pull against each other.
extra_html:
Spec first, geometry second

WorldClaw's answer is to make the plan an explicit artifact. Planning agents turn the open-ended prompt into a structured specification: regions, terrain, assets, materials, and the spatial relations among them. Only then does generation start, coarse to fine. A terrain foundation is assembled from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative or procedural materials, and a region-aware height field — this is what holds global coherence.

Regions that demand detail get terrain-conditioned compositions, which are reconstructed into editable textured meshes with their placement back on the terrain recovered. Render-based agents then close the loop, refining terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts against what the scene actually looks like when rendered. Guo and colleagues report that across diverse open-world prompts the result keeps a consistent global terrain structure while still yielding instance-level editable assets — the property that separates a usable world from a pretty one.

related.title: SpatialClaw: Code as the Action Interface for Spatial Reasoning
related.hook: Give a vision-language agent a live Python kernel instead of a fixed tool menu, and let it write one cell at a time. That flexibility lifts 3D/4D spatial reasoning by 11 points.

related.title: Motion Has Geometry Too
related.hook: Tracking and optical flow treat every pixel as drifting on its own. But real objects are rigid — points on the same body move together, so give motion a basis instead of a per-pixel guess.

flashcards.prompt: What three requirements make large-scale text-to-3D world generation hard?
flashcards.back_html: Maintaining global spatial coherence across the whole world, producing rich local content within it, and emitting explicit assets that can still be edited and reused downstream — all at the same time.

flashcards.prompt: What do WorldClaw's planning agents produce from the text prompt?

choices.text: A structured specification of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations
A rendered preview image that the rest of the pipeline lifts into 3D
A sequence of camera trajectories through the world to be generated

flashcards.explanation_html: The spec comes first and everything else is built against it — that's what gives the coarse-to-fine pipeline a global structure to stay coherent with as it fills in local detail.

flashcards.prompt: Why does it matter that WorldClaw outputs instance-level editable meshes?
flashcards.back_html: A baked scene can only be looked at. Editable textured meshes with recovered placement on the terrain can be modified, reused, and pulled into downstream pipelines — which is what makes a generated world usable rather than just viewable.
